docs.title: Welcome to CogniAgents
docs.text: CogniAgents is a YAML-driven framework for creating and managing AI agents. It is designed to be simple, maintainable, and extensible, allowing you to build powerful AI-native applications with just a config.yaml file.

docs.title: About the Framework
docs.text:
CogniAgents is built on the idea that the core components of an AI application—agents, tools, and schemas—should be defined in a declarative, human-readable format. This makes it easy to manage your application's configuration, version it with Git, and collaborate with your team.

At its core, CogniAgents uses the powerful PydanticAI library to handle the interaction with the LLM, giving you a robust and reliable engine for your agents.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text: Getting started with CogniAgents is easy. Here are the basic steps to create and run your first agent.

docs.title: 1. Installation
docs.text: pip install cogni-agents

docs.title: 2. Create Your config.yaml
docs.text:
Create a config.yaml file in the root of your project:

global_llm_settings:
  model: "gemini-2.5-flash"

agents:
  - name: hello_agent
    description: "A simple agent that says hello."
    prompt: |
      Say hello to {name}.
    output_schema: "string"

This configuration defines a single agent named hello_agent that takes a name as input and returns a string.

docs.title: 3. Run Your Agent
docs.text:
Create a Python script to run your agent:

import asyncio
from cogni_agents.cogni_agent import CogniAgent
from cogni_agents.config_loader import set_config_path

# Set the path to your configuration file
set_config_path("config.yaml")

async def main():
    agent = await CogniAgent.from_name("hello_agent")
    result = await agent.invoke({"name": "World"})
    print(result.output)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

When you run this script, you should see the following output:

Hello, World!

docs.title: Next Steps
docs.text:
Now that you have created your first agent, you are ready to explore the more advanced features of the CogniAgents framework:

  • Core Concepts: Learn about the fundamental building blocks of the framework, including agents, tools, and schemas.
  • Adding Tools: Discover how to add custom Python functions as tools for your agents to use.
  • Built-in Schemas: See the list of built-in schemas that you can use for structured output.

docs.title: 1. Overview
docs.text:
CogniAgents is a generic, config-driven agentic framework built on:

  • PydanticAI for typed, structured LLM agents
  • An OpenAI-compatible endpoint (e.g., OpenWebUI) as the model backend
  • A flexible config.yaml to declare agents, workflows, and templates

The framework is not limited to news aggregation. It’s designed to support many AI workflows, such as:

  • Document & email summarization
  • Trend, risk, or sentiment analysis
  • Data extraction & normalization
  • Code review & explanation
  • Content generation (blog posts, reports, social posts)
  • Internal tools (ticket triage, routing, classification)

The core idea: you describe what agents exist and how workflows are composed in config.yaml. CogniAgents turns that into an executable pipeline using PydanticAI and your OpenWebUI models.

docs.title: 2.1 Goals
docs.text:
1. Generic: Support arbitrary domains (news, finance, code, customer service, etc.).
  2. Config-driven:
  3. Agents, prompts, models, and workflows live in config.yaml.
  4. Minimal code changes when you add or modify behavior.
  5. OpenWebUI-compatible:
  6. Talk to any OpenAI-compatible API (OpenWebUI) via OPENAI_BASE_URL / OPENAI_API_KEY.
  7. Typed with PydanticAI:
  8. Structured outputs where needed (Pydantic models).
  9. Plain strings where simple outputs are enough.
  10. Compositional workflows:
  11. Chain multiple agents in a configurable workflow (sequential or parallel).
  12. Extensible:
  13. Easy to add new agents, output schemas, and workflows.

docs.title: 2.2 Non-Goals (v1)
docs.text:
• Full autonomous planning / tool-calling orchestration (ReAct, etc.).
  • Long-term memory and retrieval-augmented generation.
  • Multi-tenant management (per-tenant configs) – can be added later.
  • Production UI for editing config (future enhancement).

docs.title: 3.1 Core Concepts
docs.text:
• Agent: A PydanticAI Agent with:
  • name, description
  • model (OpenWebUI model name)
  • instructions/prompt
  • output type (str or a Pydantic model)
  • Workflow: A named, ordered set of agents plus wiring rules:
  • Which agents run
  • In what order
  • How their outputs are aggregated into a final result
  • Template (optional): A Jinja2 template that turns workflow outputs into a final string (HTML, Markdown, JSON, etc.).

docs.title: 3.2 Components
docs.text:
1. Config Loader
  2. Loads config.yaml.
  3. Validates shape via Pydantic (optional but recommended).

  4. Exposes helpers:

    • get_global_llm_settings()
    • get_agent_configs()
    • get_workflow_configs()
    • get_templates()

  5. Agent Factory / Registry

  6. Converts config entries into CogniAgent instances (wrappers around PydanticAI agents).
  7. Keeps a cache of initialized agents.

  8. Ensures lazy or eager initialization based on runtime needs.

  9. CogniAgent (Wrapper)

  10. Encapsulates:
    • PydanticAI Agent
    • The configured output type (e.g., str, SummaryOutput, TrendAnalysisOutput)

  11. Provides:

    • async invoke(input: str, context: dict | None) -> Any

  12. Workflow Engine

  13. Reads workflow definition from config.
  14. For a workflow:
    • Resolves agent list.
    • Executes agents (sequential or parallel).
    • Manages enriched_data / context object passed between steps.

  15. Optionally renders a final output via a template.

  16. Rendering Layer

  17. Jinja2 (or similar) to render templates using:

    • Workflow outputs
    • Input payload metadata
    • Global or workflow-specific context

  18. LLM Service (OpenWebUI)

  19. OpenAI-compatible API at OPENAI_BASE_URL (e.g., http://openwebui:8080/v1).
  20. Model names (e.g., gemini-2.5-flash, buffettvision, code-reviewer) are treated as opaque strings and passed through as model in the OpenAI payload.

docs.title: 4. Architecture Diagram (Mermaid)
docs.text:
flowchart TD

    subgraph Client
        A[Caller\n(API / CLI / Job\n+ Input Payload)]
    end

    subgraph Framework["CogniAgents Framework"]
        subgraph ConfigLayer
            B[Config Loader\n(config.yaml)]
        end

        subgraph AgentLayer
            C[Agent Registry\n(load & cache agents)]
            D[CogniAgent Instances\n(PydanticAI Agent wrappers)]
        end

        subgraph WorkflowLayer
            E[Workflow Engine\n(execute workflows)]
        end

        subgraph RenderLayer
            F[Template Renderer\n(Jinja2 or similar)]
        end
    end

    subgraph LLMService["LLM Service"]
        G[OpenWebUI\n(OpenAI-compatible /v1)]
    end

    A -->|workflow_name,\ninput, metadata| E
    E -->|load workflow & agent defs| B
    E -->|resolve agents| C
    C -->|ensure created| D
    E -->|invoke agents\nwith inputs & context| D
    D -->|OpenAI-compatible calls\n(model, messages)| G
    G -->|LLM responses| D
    D -->|typed outputs| E
    E -->|workflow result,\nintermediate data| F
    F -->|final rendered output\n(HTML/Markdown/JSON)| A
````

---

## 5. Config Design (`config.yaml`)

### 5.1 Top-Level Structure (Generic)

```yaml
global_llm_settings:
  model: "gemini-2.5-flash"
  temperature: 0.1

agents:
  - name: "generic_summarizer"
    title: "Generic Summarizer"
    description: "Summarizes any text content."
    llm_model: "gemini-2.5-flash"
    output_schema: "summary"     # optional hint: maps to a Pydantic model or str
    prompt: |
      Summarize the following content clearly and concisely.
      Do not refer to "this text" or "the document" in your answer.

  - name: "sentiment_analyzer"
    title: "Sentiment Analyzer"
    description: "Classifies sentiment of text."
    llm_model: "sentiment-model"
    output_schema: "sentiment"
    prompt: |
      Analyze the sentiment of the following content and return:
      - overall sentiment (positive, neutral, negative)
      - a short rationale.

  - name: "code_reviewer"
    title: "Code Reviewer"
    description: "Reviews code snippets."
    llm_model: "code-reviewer"
    output_schema: "code_review"
    prompt: |
      You are a senior engineer. Review the following code and provide:
      - key issues
      - suggested improvements
      - overall risk level.

workflows:
  - name: "summarize_document"
    description: "Summarize arbitrary input text."
    steps:
      - agent: "generic_summarizer"
        input_from: "payload.content"   # where to get input
        save_as: "summary"              # key in workflow context

  - name: "analyze_text_with_sentiment"
    description: "Summarize and analyze sentiment."
    steps:
      - agent: "generic_summarizer"
        input_from: "payload.content"
        save_as: "summary"
      - agent: "sentiment_analyzer"
        input_from: "payload.content"
        save_as: "sentiment"

  - name: "review_code_snippet"
    description: "Run code review on a snippet."
    steps:
      - agent: "code_reviewer"
        input_from: "payload.code"
        save_as: "review"

templates:
  # Example: generic HTML/Markdown templates keyed by workflow name
  summarize_document: |
    # Summary

    {{ summary }}

  analyze_text_with_sentiment: |
    # Summary

    {{ summary }}

    # Sentiment

    Overall sentiment: {{ sentiment.sentiment }}
    Rationale: {{ sentiment.rationale }}

defaults:
  # Default options that can be used by workflows/callers
  max_tokens: 2048
  language: "en"

Note: output_schema is a logical name that the framework maps to:

  • str for simple text outputs, or
  • Pydantic models like SummaryOutput, SentimentOutput, CodeReviewOutput.

docs.title: 6.1 Config Loader
docs.text:
Responsibilities:

  • Load config.yaml once (with optional hot-reload in dev).
  • Provide typed accessors:
def get_global_llm_settings() -> dict: ...
def get_agent_configs() -> list[dict]: ...
def get_workflow_configs() -> list[dict]: ...
def get_template(workflow_name: str) -> str | None: ...

Optional: use Pydantic to validate config structure.

docs.title: 6.2 Output Schemas (Pydantic Models)
docs.text:
Example schema registry:

from typing import Type, Dict, Union
from pydantic import BaseModel


class SummaryOutput(BaseModel):
    summary: str


class SentimentOutput(BaseModel):
    sentiment: str
    rationale: str


class CodeReviewOutput(BaseModel):
    issues: list[str]
    suggestions: list[str]
    risk_level: str


# Map logical schema names to actual Python types
OUTPUT_SCHEMAS: Dict[str, Type[BaseModel] | Type[str]] = {
    "summary": SummaryOutput,
    "sentiment": SentimentOutput,
    "code_review": CodeReviewOutput,
    # default: str if not present
}

docs.title: 6.3 CogniAgent Wrapper
docs.text:
import logging
from typing import Any, Dict, Type

from pydantic_ai import Agent as PydanticAIAgent
from pydantic_ai.models.openai import OpenAIChatModel

from .config_loader import get_global_llm_settings
from .schemas import OUTPUT_SCHEMAS  # mapping from output_schema -> type

logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)


class CogniAgent:
    def __init__(self, agent_config: Dict[str, Any]):
        self.name = agent_config["name"]
        self.title = agent_config.get("title", self.name)
        self.description = agent_config.get("description")
        self.prompt = agent_config["prompt"]
        self.llm_model = agent_config["llm_model"]
        self.temperature = agent_config.get("temperature")
        self.output_schema_name = agent_config.get("output_schema")

        global_llm = get_global_llm_settings()
        model_name = self.llm_model or global_llm.get("model")
        if model_name is None:
            raise ValueError(f"Agent '{self.name}' missing model name.")

        self.output_type: Type[Any] = OUTPUT_SCHEMAS.get(
            self.output_schema_name, str
        )

        temp = (
            self.temperature
            if self.temperature is not None
            else global_llm.get("temperature", 0.1)
        )

        chat_model = OpenAIChatModel(model_name)

        self.agent = PydanticAIAgent(
            chat_model,
            instructions=self._build_instructions(),
            output_type=self.output_type,
            model_settings={"temperature": temp},
        )

        logger.info(
            f"Initialized CogniAgent '{self.name}' with model={model_name}, "
            f"output_type={self.output_type}"
        )

    def _build_instructions(self) -> str:
        # Optionally enrich the base prompt with schema hints
        # For simple cases, just return the prompt.
        return self.prompt

    async def invoke(self, input_text: str, context: Dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> Any:
        # `context` can be used later if you want to incorporate more info
        result = await self.agent.run(input_text)
        return result.output

docs.title: 6.4 Agent Registry
docs.text:
import asyncio
from typing import Dict

from .config_loader import get_agent_configs
from .cogni_agent import CogniAgent

_agents: Dict[str, CogniAgent] = {}
_loaded = False
_lock = asyncio.Lock()


async def ensure_agents_loaded():
    global _loaded
    if _loaded:
        return

    async with _lock:
        if _loaded:
            return

        for cfg in get_agent_configs():
            name = cfg["name"]
            _agents[name] = CogniAgent(cfg)

        _loaded = True


def get_agent(name: str) -> CogniAgent:
    return _agents[name]

docs.title: 6.5 Workflow Engine
docs.text:
from typing import Any, Dict

from .config_loader import get_workflow_configs, get_template
from .agent_registry import ensure_agents_loaded, get_agent

# workflow configs indexed by name for quick lookup
_workflow_by_name: Dict[str, Dict[str, Any]] = {}


async def load_workflows():
    global _workflow_by_name
    if _workflow_by_name:
        return
    for wf in get_workflow_configs():
        _workflow_by_name[wf["name"]] = wf


async def run_workflow(workflow_name: str, payload: Dict[str, Any]) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    await ensure_agents_loaded()
    await load_workflows()

    wf = _workflow_by_name[workflow_name]
    context: Dict[str, Any] = {"payload": payload, "results": {}}

    for step in wf["steps"]:
        agent_name = step["agent"]
        input_path = step.get("input_from", "payload.content")
        save_as = step.get("save_as", agent_name)

        agent = get_agent(agent_name)
        # resolve input from context via a simple dotted path
        input_text = _resolve_path(context, input_path)

        result = await agent.invoke(input_text, context=context)
        context["results"][save_as] = result

    return context


def _resolve_path(ctx: Dict[str, Any], path: str) -> str:
    parts = path.split(".")
    val: Any = ctx
    for p in parts:
        val = val[p]
    return val


def render_workflow_output(workflow_name: str, context: Dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    template_str = get_template(workflow_name)
    if not template_str:
        # default: return results as a string
        return str(context["results"])

    # Jinja2 environment should be created elsewhere and cached
    from jinja2 import Template
    template = Template(template_str)
    return template.render(**context["results"], payload=context["payload"])

docs.title: 7. Execution Flow (Example)
docs.text:
1. Caller invokes CogniAgents with:

  2. workflow_name="analyze_text_with_sentiment"

  3. payload={"content": "Some arbitrary text..."}

  4. run_workflow:

  5. Ensures agents & workflows are loaded from config.yaml.

  6. Executes steps:

    • generic_summarizer → results["summary"]
    • sentiment_analyzer → results["sentiment"]

  7. render_workflow_output:

  8. Uses templates.analyze_text_with_sentiment to render final Markdown/HTML.

Result: a generic, reusable, strongly-typed agentic pipeline that can be applied to any domain, not just news.

docs.title: 8. OpenWebUI Integration
docs.text:
Environment variables:

  • OPENAI_BASE_URL="http://openwebui:8080/v1"
  • OPENAI_API_KEY="your-token-or-dummy"

PydanticAI’s OpenAIChatModel(model_name):

  • Sends {"model": "<llm_model from config.yaml>", "messages": [...]} to OPENAI_BASE_URL.
  • OpenWebUI routes the request to the appropriate backend model.

This makes CogniAgents backend-agnostic as long as the backend speaks OpenAI’s API dialect.

docs.title: 9. Future Enhancements
docs.text:
• Parallel step execution:

  • Allow parallel: true in workflow steps and run agents concurrently.

  • Tool-using agents:

  • Use PydanticAI tools for external data (APIs, DBs, search).

  • Multi-tenant configs:

  • Support multiple config.yaml files, one per tenant/project.

  • Hot reload in dev:

  • Watch config.yaml and reload agents/workflows on change.

  • Config UI:

  • Build a simple web UI to edit agents, workflows, and templates.

This design makes CogniAgents a generic, reusable agentic framework that can power everything from your news aggregation use case to code review, support triage, and beyond — all while staying OpenWebUI-compatible and config-driven.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: Contributions are welcome! We appreciate your help in making CogniAgents better.

docs.title: Bug Reports & Feature Requests
docs.text:
If you encounter a bug or have an idea for a new feature, please open an issue on our GitHub repository.

Please provide as much detail as possible: - For bugs: Steps to reproduce, expected behavior, actual behavior, and your environment. - For features: A clear description of the new functionality and its use case.

docs.title: Development Process
docs.text:
1. Fork the repository on GitHub.
  2. Clone your fork locally: git clone https://github.com/your-username/CogniAgents.git
  3. Create a new branch for your changes: git checkout -b feature/my-new-feature or fix/a-specific-bug.
  4. Make your changes. Ensure you add or update docstrings and tests where appropriate.
  5. Run tests to ensure everything is working correctly: pytest.
  6. Commit your changes with a descriptive commit message.
  7. Push your branch to your fork: git push origin feature/my-new-feature.
  8. Open a Pull Request from your fork to the main CogniAgents repository.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text: The CogniAgents framework is built on a few fundamental concepts that work together to create powerful, configuration-driven AI systems. Understanding these concepts is key to using the framework effectively.

docs.title: 1. The Configuration File (config.yaml)
docs.text:
The config.yaml file is the heart of a CogniAgents application. It is where you define all the components of your system in a declarative, human-readable format. A typical configuration file has the following top-level sections:

  • global_llm_settings: Default values for the LLM that can be inherited by agents.
  • agents: A list of all the individual AI agents you want to define.
  • custom_schemas: Pointers to custom Pydantic models for structured agent outputs.
  • custom_tools: Pointers to custom Python functions that can be used as tools by agents.
  • mcp_servers: Configuration for any MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers that provide additional tools as toolsets.
  • prompt_components: Reusable snippets of text that can be included in agent prompts.

docs.title: 2. Agents
docs.text:
An Agent is the basic building block of the framework. It is a specialized AI entity designed to perform a single, well-defined task. For example, you might have an agent that summarizes text, another that analyzes sentiment, and a third that categorizes customer support tickets.

An agent is defined in the agents section of your config.yaml.

docs.title: Example Agent Definition:
docs.text:
agents:
  - name: sentiment_analyzer
    description: "Analyzes the sentiment of a customer review."
    llm:
      temperature: 0.0
    prompt: |
      Analyze the sentiment of the following text and classify it as 'positive', 'negative', or 'neutral'.
      Provide a brief justification for your classification.
      Text: {text_to_analyze}
    output_schema: "SentimentOutput" # References a built-in or custom schema

docs.title: Key Agent Properties:
docs.text:
• name: A unique identifier for the agent.
  • description: A brief explanation of what the agent does.
  • llm: Agent-specific settings for the LLM, which override the global_llm_settings.
  • prompt: The instructions for the agent, including placeholders for input.
  • output_schema: The name of the schema that defines the agent's output structure.
  • tools: A list of the names of the local custom tools that the agent can use.
  • toolsets: A list of the names of the MCP servers that the agent can use as toolsets.

docs.title: 3. Schemas
docs.text:
A Schema defines the structure of an agent's output. By enforcing a schema, you ensure that the LLM's response is predictable, structured, and easy to work with in your application. Schemas are defined using Pydantic models.

The framework includes several built-in schemas, but you can easily define your own.

docs.title: Custom Schema Definition:
docs.text:
To use a custom schema, you define it in a Python file and reference it from your config.yaml.

my_app/schemas.py:

from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class SupportRoute(BaseModel):
    department: str = Field(description="The department to route to (e.g., 'Billing', 'Technical Support', 'Sales').")
    urgency: int = Field(description="An urgency score from 1 to 5.")

config.yaml:

custom_schemas:
  support_route_schema: "my_app.schemas.SupportRoute"

agents:
  - name: support_router
    ...
    output_schema: support_route_schema # Use the custom schema

docs.title: 4. Tools and Toolsets
docs.text:
Tools and Toolsets are how you give your agents the ability to interact with the outside world. They can be used to retrieve information, perform calculations, or trigger external processes.

  • Tools: A tool is a single, callable Python function that you define locally in your project.
  • Toolsets: A toolset is a collection of tools that are exposed by an MCP server.

docs.title: Custom Tool Definition:
docs.text:
my_app/tools.py:

def get_current_time() -> str:
    """Returns the current time."""
    from datetime import datetime
    return datetime.now().isoformat()

config.yaml:

custom_tools:
  get_time: "my_app.tools.get_current_time"

agents:
  - name: time_agent
    ...
    tools:
      - get_time

docs.title: MCP Toolset Definition:
docs.text:
config.yaml:

mcp_servers:
  remote_fetcher:
    type: "streamable-http"
    url: "https://remote.mcpservers.org/fetch/mcp"

agents:
  - name: fetcher_agent
    ...
    toolsets:
      - remote_fetcher

docs.title: 5. Prompt Components
docs.text: Prompt Components are reusable pieces of text that help you keep your prompts DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself). You can define a component once and reference it in multiple agent prompts.

docs.title: Example Prompt Component:
docs.text:
config.yaml:

prompt_components:
  politeness_clause: "Be polite and professional in your response."

agents:
  - name: sentiment_analyzer
    prompt: |
      Analyze the sentiment of the following text.
      {{ prompt_components.politeness_clause }}

docs.title: Guide: Adding Tools to Agents
docs.text: This guide explains how to add functionality to your agents by using local custom tools and by connecting to MCP (Model Context Protocol) servers.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before you begin, you should have a basic CogniAgents application set up with a config.yaml file and a Python script to run your agents. If you haven't done this yet, please see the Getting Started guide.

docs.title: Tools vs. Toolsets
docs.text:
In the CogniAgents framework, tools and toolsets are distinct concepts:

  • Tools: A tool is a single, callable Python function that you define locally in your project. Each tool is registered individually in the custom_tools section of your config.yaml and is added to an agent's tools list.

  • Toolsets: A toolset is a collection of tools that are exposed by an MCP server. You define the connection to the MCP server in the mcp_servers section of your config.yaml, and you add the server to an agent's toolsets list. The agent can then access all the tools provided by that server.

In short, tools are for a la carte, local functions, while toolsets are for consuming tools from an external MCP server.

docs.title: Adding Local Custom Tools
docs.text: Here’s how to create and add a local custom tool to an agent.

docs.title: 1. Create a Custom Tool
docs.text:
A tool is a simple Python function. Let's create a tool that retrieves the current weather for a given location.

Create a file, for example, my_app/tools.py:

import random

def get_current_weather(location: str) -> str:
    """Gets the current weather for a given location."""
    if "tokyo" in location.lower():
        return f"The current weather in Tokyo is 20°C and sunny."
    elif "san francisco" in location.lower():
        return f"The current weather in San Francisco is 15°C and foggy."
    else:
        return f"The current weather in {location} is {random.randint(10, 30)}°C."

docs.title: 2. Register the Tool
docs.text:
Now, let's register our tool in the config.yaml file.

custom_tools:
  weather_tool: "my_app.tools:get_current_weather"

docs.title: 3. Use the Tool in an Agent
docs.text:
Finally, we can use the tool in an agent by adding the tool's name to the tools list in the agent's configuration.

agents:
  - name: weather_agent
    description: "An agent that can retrieve the current weather."
    prompt: |
      What is the current weather in {location}?
    tools:
      - weather_tool
    output_schema: "string"

docs.title: 4. Putting It All Together
docs.text:
Here is the complete config.yaml and run_agent.py for this example:

config.yaml:

global_llm_settings:
  model: "gemini-2.5-flash"

custom_tools:
  weather_tool: "my_app.tools:get_current_weather"

agents:
  - name: weather_agent
    description: "An agent that can retrieve the current weather."
    prompt: |
      What is the current weather in {location}?
    tools:
      - weather_tool
    output_schema: "string"

run_agent.py:

import asyncio
from cogni_agents.cogni_agent import CogniAgent
from cogni_agents.config_loader import set_config_path

# Set the path to your configuration file
set_config_path("config.yaml")

async def main():
    agent = await CogniAgent.from_name("weather_agent")
    result = await agent.invoke({"location": "San Francisco"})
    print(result.output)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Connecting to MCP Servers
docs.text: Here’s how to connect to an MCP server and use its tools as a toolset.

docs.title: 1. Configure the MCP Server
docs.text:
First, you need to add an mcp_servers section to your config.yaml file.

mcp_servers:
  my_mcp_server:
    type: "streamable-http"
    url: "https://remote.mcpservers.org/fetch/mcp"

docs.title: 2. Use the MCP Toolset in an Agent
docs.text:
Next, you can add the MCP server to an agent's toolsets list:

agents:
  - name: my_agent
    description: "An agent that can use tools from an MCP server."
    prompt: |
      Fetch the content of {url}
    toolsets:
      - my_mcp_server
    output_schema: "string"

docs.title: 3. Putting It All Together
docs.text:
Here is the complete config.yaml and run_agent.py for this example:

config.yaml:

global_llm_settings:
  model: "gemini-2.5-flash"

mcp_servers:
  my_mcp_server:
    type: "streamable-http"
    url: "https://remote.mcpservers.org/fetch/mcp"

agents:
  - name: my_agent
    description: "An agent that can use tools from an MCP server."
    prompt: |
      Fetch the content of {url}
    toolsets:
      - my_mcp_server
    output_schema: "string"

run_agent.py:

import asyncio
from cogni_agents.cogni_agent import CogniAgent
from cogni_agents.config_loader import set_config_path

# Set the path to your configuration file
set_config_path("config.yaml")

async def main():
    agent = await CogniAgent.from_name("my_agent")
    result = await agent.invoke({"url": "http://example.com"})
    print(result.output)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    asyncio.run(main())

docs.title: Reference: Built-in Schemas
docs.text: The CogniAgents framework includes several pre-defined schemas for common AI tasks. You can use these in your agent definitions by referencing their short names in the output_schema field, without needing to define a custom schema.

docs.title: str
docs.text:
The most basic output type, representing a single, unstructured string of text.

  • Name in config: str
  • Use Case: Ideal for agents that generate freeform text, like creative writing, drafting an email, or providing a simple answer.
  • Output Type: string
  • Example Agent Config: 
    agents:
  - name: simple_responder
    prompt: "Answer the user's question concisely. Question: {question}"
    output_schema: "str"

docs.title: summary
docs.text:
A structured schema for summarizing text, specifically designed to separate positive and negative aspects.

  • Name in config: summary
  • Use Case: Perfect for analyzing product reviews, user feedback, or any text where you need to extract pros and cons.
  • Schema Definition: 
    class SummaryOutput(BaseModel):
    positive_aspects: List[str]
    negative_aspects: List[str]
  • Example Agent Config: 
    agents:
  - name: review_summarizer
    prompt: "Summarize the key positive and negative points from this review: {review_text}"
    output_schema: "summary"

docs.title: sentiment
docs.text:
A structured schema for sentiment analysis.

  • Name in config: sentiment
  • Use Case: Classifying a piece of text as positive, negative, or neutral, and requiring the agent to provide a justification for its decision.
  • Schema Definition: 
    class SentimentOutput(BaseModel):
    sentiment: str  # e.g., "positive", "neutral", "negative"
    rationale: str  # A short explanation for the sentiment
  • Example Agent Config: 
    agents:
  - name: sentiment_analyzer
    prompt: "Analyze the sentiment of this comment: {comment_text}"
    output_schema: "sentiment"

docs.title: code_review
docs.text:
A structured schema for performing a high-level automated code review.

  • Name in config: code_review
  • Use Case: Analyzing a code snippet to identify potential issues, suggest improvements, and assess the overall risk level. This is useful for automated quality checks.
  • Schema Definition: 
    class CodeReviewOutput(BaseModel):
    issues: List[str]
    suggestions: List[str]
    risk_level: str # e.g., "low", "medium", "high"
  • Example Agent Config: 
    agents:
  - name: basic_code_reviewer
    prompt: "Review the following code for issues and suggest improvements: {code_snippet}"
    output_schema: "code_review"
